title: Static onboarding tours break. The real cost of maintaining them in 2026.
summary: Product tours need checking as screens and permissions change. Include that work when evaluating a tour tool, and choose where authored flows or generated guidance fit the task.
body_markdown:
An[onboarding tour](https://frigade.com/glossary/product-tour) becomes part of the product you need to maintain. When a screen changes, someone has to check that the tour still points to the right controls and that its instructions still make sense.


We build tools for authored tours in Frigade Engage, as well as generated guidance in Frigade Assistant. Both have a place. Choosing between them starts with how often the workflow changes and how much control you need over the experience.


## The numbers nobody runs


When you evaluate a[tours product](https://productonboarding.com/articles/how-to-build-product-tours) , include the time to check and repair the flows you publish. The subscription price covers access to the software. Your team still needs to verify the experience inside your product.


For a simple planning example, suppose you have twelve tours and spend ten minutes checking each one every month. That is two hours a month before repairs. If you check separate versions for admins and members, budget for both. These are illustrative inputs, not a benchmark for what a typical team spends.


Repair time depends on the change. A renamed button might require one edit. A workflow that moves to another page could require rebuilding several steps and checking them with different accounts.


Measure this during a trial if you can. Build a tour for a workflow you expect to change, then revisit it after a release. Record the time to identify the affected steps, repair them, and verify the result. That gives you a maintenance estimate tied to your product.


## Why this happens


A tour step can use a CSS selector to identify the element it should highlight. If it targets` .btn-primary` and a refactor removes that class, the selector no longer finds the intended button. A more stable data attribute can help, provided the team maintains it along with the component.


A step can also become wrong while its target remains intact. Suppose a tour tells someone to invite a colleague, but invitations now require an owner's approval. The tooltip may appear in the correct place and still describe a task that person cannot complete.


Feature flags and account state add cases to check. A new account may need to create a project before it can import data. An existing account may already be on the import screen. One sequence of instructions needs conditions or separate paths if it is going to serve both.


Give each tour an owner and include it when reviewing changes to the workflow it describes. Stable selectors help with locating controls; checking the instructions against the task catches a different class of problem.


## What changed in 2026


Generated guidance gives you another option for help that begins with a customer's question. Frigade Assistant learns workflows by using your product and can[generate a walkthrough](https://frigade.com/features/ai-generated-tours) for the task someone needs help with. As it relearns the product, that knowledge can inform updated guidance.


This still needs review. The learning account must have access to the relevant experience, and your team should check the guidance after a substantial change. Generated help is useful only if it gets someone through the current workflow.


An authored flow remains useful when you want to choose the exact message and sequence. A welcome checklist or a short introduction to a new feature may deserve that control. Frigade Engage supports those experiences, and using an assistant does not require removing them.


You can make the choice per workflow. Keep the authored introduction where the sequence matters. Try generated guidance for tasks with several paths or questions that arrive after onboarding is over.


## What traditional product tours actually cost


The cost includes authoring, verification, and repair. It also includes deciding when a tour no longer belongs in the product. An old announcement can keep working exactly as built and still be irrelevant to the people seeing it.


Before adding a flow, name who will maintain it and which product changes should trigger a review. If you cannot give it that attention, limit it to a shorter, more stable part of the experience.


Use the next release to test the arrangement. Check whether customers can finish the task and how much work keeping that guidance accurate required. Those results will tell you where to keep an authored tour and where to try a different approach.


## Why do onboarding tours need maintenance?


Tours need review when controls move, instructions change, or different accounts follow different paths. Stable selectors can reduce targeting failures, but someone still needs to check that each step is relevant and that the intended audience can complete the task.
